This is blowing my mind.

Is this true, you can't run Postgres or MySQL in Claude Code and Cursor?

You can run your full stack in orbs. We run multiple dev servers/services, Postgres, Redis, Docker in there.

And hard disagree on 2nd point: the "problems of remote coding" *are* solved.

For one, you're no longer coding :) No need anymore to get LSPs or other editor-centric tooling running. Or an editor! That was always a huge pain in the ass, now the whole ass is gone.

And everything else that was painful about setting up remote envs is truly no longer painful with agents. Configuring services to work in there, making headless browsers work, making headless anything work -- super easy now.

It sounds like Armin & Ben haven't tried it, but I urge you: put your code on a remote box, headless, ask an agent to run through it end to end. It will blow your mind.

Everything has changed.

hits.name: Zach Lloyd
hits.text:
Most of the influential twitter folks criticizing software factories work at companies that make coding agents and don't have a factory platform (Warp has both). So there's a natural thing happening here that's like "we don't offer a factory thing, therefore that thing must not be real."

But this is backwards: it's the coding agent market that is commoditized and the factory challenge is what matters. 

The challenge right now isn't how to build a good coding agent or local agent workbench or even a personal swarm of agents, it's how do you scale coding agents efficiently across an organization so that every engineer on your team can get the most out of them and the business itself can be confident that this new magic technology they are spending a ton of money on is being deployed efficiently and securely. 

Every platform team I talk to wants a solution for this; no one is clamoring for more coding agents or better local workbenches.

hits.text:
8 AI model architectures, visually explained:

LLMs get so much attention that it's easy to overlook the rest of the field. Different inputs, tasks, and deployment constraints have led to very different model designs.

Here are eight specialized AI model architectures:

1. LLM (Large language models)

Text is split into tokens, mapped to embeddings, and processed through transformer layers. The model generates its response by predicting successive tokens.

↳ GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama.

2. LCM (Large concept models)

Moves prediction to the sentence level. Sentences become SONAR embeddings, and the model predicts the next sentence representation. Meta explored both autoregressive and diffusion-based versions.

↳ Meta's LCM research introduced this approach.

3. LAM (Large action models)

Connects a user's request to actions in an environment. These systems interpret intent, plan steps, and use interfaces or tools, often checking results before continuing.

↳ Rabbit R1, Microsoft UFO, Claude Computer Use.

4. MoE (Mixture of experts)

A router assigns token representations to selected expert networks inside the model. Activating a subset of experts adds model capacity without running every expert for every token.

↳ Mixtral, DeepSeek, Switch Transformer.

5. VLM (Vision-language models)

Combines visual representations with language processing. A vision encoder extracts image features, which are connected to a language model so it can answer questions about visual content.

↳ GPT-4V, Gemini, LLaVA.

6. SLM (Small language models)

Uses fewer parameters to reduce memory and compute requirements. These models can run locally, with quantization often reducing their deployment footprint further.

↳ Phi-3, Gemma, Mistral 7B, Llama 3.2 1B.

7. MLM (Masked language models)

Learns by predicting hidden tokens using context on both sides. This bidirectional training produces representations useful for retrieval, classification, and other language-understanding tasks.

↳ BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa.

8. SAM (Segment Anything Model)

An image encoder processes the image, while a prompt encoder handles points, boxes, or masks. A mask decoder combines them to identify the requested regions.

↳ Meta's SAM supports interactive segmentation and image annotation.

These aren't eight mutually exclusive categories. A small model can process images, and a language model can use MoE layers. Some labels describe architecture, while others describe training or intended use.

There's another approach I kept outside the image because it alters how a model handles context rather than introducing a separate model family.

Recursive language models, from MIT, put the input into a Python environment that a root model can inspect through code.

The model can search or slice that input, then make recursive model calls on selected portions instead of loading everything into its own context window.

The reported experiments handled inputs beyond 10 million tokens without retraining, with gains over the base model even on some tasks whose inputs already fit its context window.

I recently wrote a full breakdown of how this works, including why accessing a large input and reasoning reliably over it are different problems.

Read it below.

virals.text:
I use Hermes, Claude Code and Codex every day. 

Each one is great on its own. The painful part is everything in between: copying the plan or progress from one to the other, pasting diffs, explaining the error again, and hoping they don't overwrite each other's files.

So I built Thoth, a Hermes plugin that makes them work as one team, each with its own harness. 🙌

Why not one super-agent "supervisor", or one wrapper around all of them? 

Because the harnesses are already really good. Hermes, Claude Code and Codex each come with their own tools, sandboxes, sub-agents and models, built by the people who know them best

I don't want to replace any of that. What's missing is how they work together. That's what Thoth is for.

What you get:
• No copy-paste: what one agent decides or makes goes straight into the next one's brief
• They check each other's work, so bugs get caught before they reach main
• Nothing runs or merges without your OK, and every agent runs on your own logins and plans
• Each agent gets its own workspace, so they can work side by side without breaking each other's work
• A live canvas right beside your Hermes chat, plus a Team & brain view of who did what
• Not only code: art, docs, research, and a clean Chrome （or you can even use your own chrome) when a task needs the web
• Whatever @claudeai , @ChatGPT  and @NousResearch  ship to their harnesses reaches your team the day it ships

The numbers, from Thoth's own records:
• 92% of prompt tokens came from cache in this run
• 99% of the agents' transcripts stayed out of Hermes's context, so the coordinator stays light
• On a CRM we built both ways: 26% fewer tokens and 35% faster than passing work between agents by hand

Today the team is Hermes, Claude Code and Codex. Next I want any agent with its own harness to join the same board ( Deepseek & Grok bot soon) 

Built for the @NousResearch @Teknium  Hermes Agent plugin hackathon ：https://t.co/o2j30aFIZo

Because the harnesses are already really good. Hermes, Claude Code and Codex each come with their own tools, sandboxes, sub-agents and models, built by the people who know them best

I don't want to replace any of that. What's missing is how they work together. That's what Thoth is for.

What you get:
• No copy-paste: what one agent decides or makes goes straight into the next one's brief
• They check each other's work, so bugs get caught before they reach main
